assign-cookies.pattern: Greedy matching after sorting (smallest cookie that satisfies the least greedy child)

approaches.name: For each child, search all cookies for the smallest that fits
approaches.idea: Serve children from least to most greedy; give each the smallest unused cookie that satisfies them, found by scanning every cookie.
steps: Sort `g`. Keep a `used` flag per cookie.
For each child, scan all cookies for the smallest unused `s[j] >= g[i]`.
If found, mark it used and count the child.
approaches.why: Each of the n children scans m cookies. The flags take O(m).

approaches.name: Sort both and match with two pointers
approaches.idea: With both lists sorted, walk the cookies from small to large. Each cookie goes to the least greedy unserved child if it is big enough; otherwise it is too small for everyone left, so skip it.
steps: Sort `g` and `s`. Set `child = 0`.
For each cookie in increasing size: if `child < g.length` and the cookie is `>= g[child]`, serve that child (`child++`).
Return `child`, the number of content children.
approaches.time: O(n log n + m log m)
approaches.why: Two sorts and one linear pass (aside from the sorts' own memory). Using the smallest cookie that works never hurts: any larger cookie saved is at least as useful later.

best-time-to-buy-and-sell-stock.pattern: One pass tracking the minimum so far (best sale = today − cheapest earlier day)

approaches.name: Try every buy day and sell day
approaches.idea: Check every pair of days `i < j` and keep the largest `prices[j] − prices[i]`.
steps: Set `best = 0`.
For each `i` and each `j > i`, update `best` with `prices[j] − prices[i]`.
Return `best`.
approaches.why: n(n − 1)/2 pairs; for n = 10⁵ that is 5 × 10⁹.

approaches.name: Track the cheapest price so far
approaches.idea: If you sell on day `j`, the best buy day is the cheapest day before it. So scan once, remembering the lowest price seen, and check the profit of selling today.
steps: Set `minPrice = ∞`, `best = 0`.
For each price: update `best` with `price − minPrice`, then update `minPrice`.
Return `best`.
approaches.why: One pass with two variables. Updating `best` before `minPrice` ensures you never sell on the day you buy (which would only give 0 anyway).

approaches.name: Try every jump recursively
approaches.idea: From index `i`, try every jump length from 1 to `nums[i]` and see whether any of them leads to the end.
steps: `canReach(i)`: if `i` is the last index, return true.
For each step from `min(nums[i], last − i)` down to 1, if `canReach(i + step)` is true, return true.
Return false. Answer `canReach(0)`.
approaches.why: The same indices are explored again and again along different paths, which can be exponential; the recursion depth is up to n.

approaches.name: DP from the right: which indices are "good"?
approaches.idea: An index is good if some jump from it lands on a good index; the last index is good. Fill this in from right to left so every answer it depends on is already known.
steps: Mark the last index good.
For `i` from n − 2 down to 0: `i` is good if any `j` in `i + 1 .. min(i + nums[i], n − 1)` is good.
Return whether index 0 is good.
approaches.why: Each index may check up to n later indices; the good/bad table is O(n).

approaches.name: Greedy: track the farthest reachable index
approaches.idea: Every index up to the farthest point reached so far is reachable. Walk forward, extending that farthest point; if you ever stand beyond it, you are stuck.
steps: Set `reach = 0`.
For each index `i`: if `i > reach`, return false.
Update `reach = max(reach, i + nums[i])`; if it reaches the last index, return true.
Return true after the loop.
approaches.why: One pass with one variable. The reachable set is always a prefix of the array, so a single number describes it.

jump-game-ii.pattern: Greedy BFS by levels (each jump count covers a window of indices)

approaches.name: DP: fewest jumps to each index
approaches.idea: `jumps[j]` = the fewest jumps to reach index `j`. From each index `i`, every index it can reach in one jump can be reached in `jumps[i] + 1`.
steps: Set `jumps[0] = 0` and every other entry to ∞.
For each `i` in order, for each `j` in `i + 1 .. min(i + nums[i], n − 1)`, set `jumps[j] = min(jumps[j], jumps[i] + 1)`.
Return `jumps[n − 1]`.
approaches.why: J = the largest jump (≤ 1000): each index relaxes up to J later indices. The table is O(n).

approaches.name: Greedy jump windows
approaches.idea: Indices reachable with exactly `j` jumps form a contiguous window. Scanning the current window, track the farthest index the next jump could reach; when the scan reaches the window's end, take a jump and the next window ends at that farthest point.
steps: Set `jumps = 0`, `end = 0` (end of the current window), `farthest = 0`.
For `i` from 0 to n − 2: `farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])`.
If `i == end`, the window is used up: `jumps++`, `end = farthest`.
Return `jumps`.
approaches.why: One pass with three variables — a breadth-first search over windows instead of single indices. The loop stops before the last index so no extra jump is counted from it.

gas-station.pattern: Greedy with running sums (a failed stretch rules out every start inside it)

approaches.name: Simulate from every start
approaches.idea: Try each station as the start and drive around, adding gas and subtracting cost; the first start whose tank never goes negative is the answer.
steps: For each start `s`, set `tank = 0`.
For `k = 0 .. n − 1`, at station `(s + k) % n` add `gas − cost`; if the tank drops below 0, this start fails.
Return the first start that completes the loop, or −1.
approaches.why: n starts, each simulating up to n stations.

approaches.name: One pass: restart after the tank runs dry
approaches.idea: If the total gas is less than the total cost, no start works. Otherwise drive from a candidate start; if the tank goes negative at station `i`, no station between the start and `i` can be the start either (each would arrive with even less fuel), so try `i + 1` next.
steps: Keep `total` (sum of all `gas − cost`), `tank` and `start = 0`.
For each `i`: add `gas[i] − cost[i]` to both `total` and `tank`.
If `tank < 0`, set `start = i + 1` and `tank = 0`.
Return `start` if `total >= 0`, else −1.
approaches.why: One pass. When the total is non-negative, the final candidate makes it to the end, and the fuel left covers the deficit of the part before it, so it completes the circle.

partition-labels.pattern: Greedy with last occurrences (extend the part to the furthest last index)

approaches.name: Find each letter's last position by scanning
approaches.idea: A part that contains a letter must extend to that letter's last occurrence. Grow the current part, finding last occurrences by scanning the string from the end each time.
steps: Start a part at `start = 0` with `end = 0`.
For each `i` in the part, find the last index of `s[i]` by scanning from the end of `s`, and set `end` to the larger of the two.
When `i == end`, the part is closed: record `end − start + 1` and start the next part at `i + 1`.
approaches.why: Each of the n positions scans the string for its letter's last index (output aside).

approaches.name: Precompute last occurrences, then one sweep
approaches.idea: Record the last index of every letter in one pass. Then sweep: the current part must reach at least the last index of every letter seen in it; once the sweep reaches that point, close the part.
steps: Fill `last[c]` with the last index of each letter.
Sweep `i` with `start` and `end`: `end = max(end, last[s[i]])`.
When `i == end`, record `end − start + 1` and set `start = i + 1`.
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the table has 26 entries. Closing a part as early as possible maximises the number of parts.

boats-to-save-people.pattern: Sort + two pointers (pair the heaviest with the lightest when possible)

approaches.name: Heaviest first, search for the heaviest partner that fits
approaches.idea: Seat the heaviest unseated person; give them the heaviest remaining partner that still fits under the limit (found by scanning), or send them alone.
steps: Sort weights descending; keep a `seated` flag per person.
For each unseated person (heaviest first): scan the remaining unseated people for the heaviest one with `weight + theirs <= limit`.
Seat both (or just the first) in one boat and count it.
approaches.why: Each boat may scan all remaining people. The flags take O(n).

approaches.name: Sort, then pair heaviest with lightest
approaches.idea: The heaviest person needs a boat no matter what. If even the lightest person cannot share it, nobody can, so they go alone; otherwise pair them with the lightest. Two pointers do this in one pass.
steps: Sort the weights; `i` at the lightest, `j` at the heaviest.
While `i <= j`: if `people[i] + people[j] <= limit`, the lightest joins (`i++`).
The heaviest always leaves in this boat (`j--`); count the boat.
approaches.why: Sorting dominates; the two-pointer pass is O(n) (aside from the sort's own memory). Pairing with the lightest is safe: if the lightest does not fit with the heaviest, no one does.

two-city-scheduling.pattern: Greedy by the difference aCost − bCost (or DP over how many went to A)

approaches.name: DP over people and the number sent to A
approaches.idea: `dp[i][a]` = the cheapest cost for the first `i` people with exactly `a` of them sent to city A. Each person goes to A or B.
steps: `dp[0][0] = 0`, everything else ∞.
For person `i` (0-based) and each count `a`: `dp[i + 1][a] = min(dp[i][a] + bCost, dp[i][a − 1] + aCost)` (when `a >= 1`).
Return `dp[2n][n]`.
approaches.why: 2n people × up to n + 1 counts, O(1) each; the table has the same size.

approaches.name: Sort by aCost − bCost
approaches.idea: Imagine first sending everyone to B. Moving a person to A changes the total by `aCost − bCost`. Exactly n people must move, so move the n with the smallest (most negative) change.
steps: Sort people by `aCost − bCost`.
Send the first n to A and the remaining n to B.
Return the sum.
approaches.why: One sort plus a linear sum (aside from the sort's own memory).

candy.pattern: Two greedy passes (left neighbours, then right neighbours), or counting slopes

approaches.name: Fix violations until none remain
approaches.idea: Start everyone at 1 candy. Repeatedly sweep the line; whenever a child has a higher rating than a neighbour but not more candies, raise them to one more than that neighbour. Stop when a sweep changes nothing.
steps: Give every child 1 candy.
Sweep: for each `i`, if `ratings[i] > ratings[i − 1]` and `candy[i] <= candy[i − 1]`, set `candy[i] = candy[i − 1] + 1`; likewise for the right neighbour.
Repeat sweeps until nothing changes; return the sum.
approaches.why: A long falling slope may need up to n sweeps of O(n) each. Raising only to the minimum needed keeps the total minimal.

approaches.name: Two passes with one array
approaches.idea: Satisfy the left-neighbour rule with a left-to-right pass, then the right-neighbour rule with a right-to-left pass, keeping the larger value so the first rule still holds.
steps: Give every child 1 candy.
Left to right: if `ratings[i] > ratings[i − 1]`, set `c[i] = c[i − 1] + 1`.
Right to left: if `ratings[i] > ratings[i + 1]`, set `c[i] = max(c[i], c[i + 1] + 1)`.
Return the sum.
approaches.why: Two linear passes and one array of n counts. Each value is the smallest that satisfies both directions, so the total is minimal.

approaches.name: One pass counting up and down slopes
approaches.idea: Candies along a rising run go 1, 2, 3, …, and along a falling run the last child gets 1 and each one before it one more. Track the current rising length `up`, falling length `down`, and the height `peak` reached before the fall; add each child's candies as you go. When a fall gets as long as the rise before it, the peak itself must grow by one too.
steps: Start with `total = 1` (the first child) and `up = down = peak = 0`.
Rising (`r[i] > r[i − 1]`): `up++`, `peak = up`, `down = 0`, add `up + 1`.
Equal: reset `up = down = peak = 0`, add 1.
Falling: `up = 0`, `down++`; add `down + 1` (each child in the fall shifts up by one, plus the new child), minus 1 if `peak >= down` (the peak is still tall enough).
approaches.why: One pass with four counters and no array. It produces the same totals as the two-pass method.
